temas.titulo: 1.1–1.2 · Thinking and working like a geographer
resumen: ## Enquiry questions
Geographers ask enquiry questions about places: **Who? What? Where? When? Why? How?**
## Geographical enquiry

A **geographical enquiry** means asking questions, using and recording geographical data and making observations to make sense of the world. The enquiry sequence: identify questions → analyse data to look for patterns and connections → reach conclusions.
The six steps of an enquiry: 1 Asking questions · 2 Collecting/recording your own data · 3 Presenting your findings · 4 Analysing your results · 5 Reaching a conclusion · 6 Evaluating your work.
## Geographical data
- **Primary data**: collected by you through **fieldwork** (photos, field sketches, surveys, questionnaires).
- **Secondary data**: collected by someone else (textbooks, newspapers, websites, published data).
- **Quantitative data**: numbers – quantities, numerical or statistical information.
- **Qualitative data**: subjective qualities, often opinions or beliefs – text, photos, sketches.
A good geographer checks the **origin, reliability and accuracy** of data and looks for **bias** (someone distorting data to promote a viewpoint).
## Why geography matters
Geographers **predict, plan and solve problems**. Employers seek geography graduates for their wider view of the world (climate disasters, migration, conflict over water resources).

resumen: ## Lines of latitude and longitude
Imaginary gridlines drawn around the world that give **co-ordinates** to fix a position.
- **Latitude**: lines that circle the Earth **from side to side**; they show how far **north or south** a place is from the **Equator (0°)**. Labelled **N** or **S**.
- **Longitude**: lines from **top to bottom** (pole to pole); they show how far **east or west** a place is from the **Prime Meridian (0°)**. Labelled **E** or **W**.
- The Equator divides the Earth into the **northern and southern hemispheres**. The Prime Meridian divides it into the **eastern and western hemispheres**.
- In **1884** the **Greenwich Observatory** (London) was chosen as the Prime Meridian.
- Latitude is always written **before** longitude: Libreville, Gabon is 0° 23'N 9° 27'E.
## The five important lines of latitude
Arctic Circle 66½°N · Tropic of Cancer 23½°N · Equator 0° · Tropic of Capricorn 23½°S · Antarctic Circle 66½°S. North Pole = 90°N, South Pole = 90°S.
## Maps and GPS
- A **political map** shows the **borders** of countries and major cities.
- A **physical map** shows **natural features** (mountains, rivers, seas).
- **GPS** (Global Positioning System) uses **24 satellites** and ground stations to work out a precise position.
- The **Degree Confluence Project** (Alex Jarrett, USA, 1996): people visit the exact spots where whole degrees of latitude and longitude meet.

temas.titulo: 1.4 · Writing like a geographer and place
resumen: ## How to write like a geographer
- **Identify the command word** (e.g. 'describe' = state what something is like).
- **Identify the geography** in the question.
- **Think and plan** before you write.
- **Use geographical words or terms** (see the Glossary).
- **Refer to data** (photos, maps, grid references, graphs).
- **Answer the six enquiry questions.**
- **Make links** between things you learn.
## Place
**Place** is one of the big ideas in geography. Every place is **different and unique**, but also **interdependent** (connected) with other places.
## Example: Scarborough

A seaside town in North Yorkshire on the east coast of England. It has a **castle on a headland**, a **bay** on each side (North Bay and South Bay), a **harbour** with **piers** and a **lighthouse**. It is changing: fewer tourists stay because more people go abroad; during the Covid-19 lockdowns there were more day-trippers.

resumen: ## The Ordnance Survey
The **Ordnance Survey (OS)** is the **national mapping agency of the United Kingdom**. It began as part of **military strategy**, mapping the **Scottish Highlands** after the rebellion in **1745**.
Geographers use maps to describe and analyse **spatial patterns** – how people, places and environments are organised. Using a map is **thinking spatially**.
## Scale
The **scale** shows how much you would have to enlarge the map to get the real size of the land. Scale is shown in three ways:
- a **linear scale** – a line marked in km;
- a **statement** – e.g. 'two centimetres represent one kilometre';
- a **ratio** – e.g. 1:50 000 means 1 unit on the map = 50 000 of the same unit on the ground.
## Large and small scale
- **Large-scale map** (e.g. 1:2500, 1:25 000): a lot of **detail** but not much **area** – individual buildings and fields.
- **Small-scale map** (e.g. 1:50 000, 1:250 000): a lot of **area** but not much detail – good for **planning routes**.
## Measuring distance
'As the crow flies' = a straight line. Distance by road is always **longer** or the same.

resumen: ## OS symbols
Symbols make maps quick to read and not cluttered. They use **colours, shapes, lines, drawings and abbreviations**. Every OS map has a **key** (legend). Different scales have different symbols.

Abbreviations: CG cattle grid · CH clubhouse · Coll college · Fm farm · Ho house · Hospl hospital · MP milepost · P post office · PC public convenience (toilets) · PH public house · Sch school · Sta station · TH town hall · Univ university.
## Grid references

OS maps are covered in numbered blue gridlines. **Eastings** are the vertical lines – their numbers increase **eastwards**. **Northings** are the horizontal lines – their numbers increase **northwards**. A grid reference is for the **bottom left-hand corner** of a square.
Remember: **along the corridor, then up the stairs** (eastings first).
## Four-figure grid reference
Read the easting at the bottom-left corner (62), then the northing (33) → **6233**.
## Six-figure grid reference
Imagine each square divided into **tenths**. Count tenths along from 62 (5 → 625) and up from 33 (3 → 333) → **625333**.

resumen: Height on OS maps is always shown in **metres above sea level**. There are three ways:
- **Spot height**: a **black dot** with the height in metres next to it.

- **Contour lines**: thin **brown** lines joining places at the **same height**. Usually every **10 m** on a 1:50 000 map and every **5 m** on a 1:25 000 map; a thicker line every **50 m**. Numbers increasing = uphill; decreasing = downhill.
- **Triangulation pillar**: a **blue triangle with a dot**, often on hilltops, with the height next to it. Once used by OS surveyors to measure the land; not used any more.
## Slopes
Contour lines **close together** = **steep** slope. Contour lines **far apart** = **gentle** slope.
Between two contour lines you can't give an exact height – only that it is between the two values.
## Compass points
N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW (north, north-east, east, south-east, south, south-west, west, north-west).

resumen: ## Aerial photos (1.8)

A **vertical aerial photograph** is taken from **directly above** the land – from an aeroplane or, more commonly, from **satellites** (e.g. Google Earth). With maps they show **physical** and **human** features and **land uses** (buildings, roads, fields, industry).
- **Urban** areas: built-up, mostly housing and industry (towns and cities, e.g. Southampton).
- **Rural** areas: more open countryside with fields.
## Models and settlements (1.9)

A **model** is a simplified version of a pattern in the real world, used to make generalisations, comparisons and predictions. Models have **exceptions** and can become **out of date**, so use them **critically**.
A **settlement** is a place where people live. More than half of the world's population lives in urban areas.

A **settlement hierarchy** orders settlements by population size, area and the range and number of services. From the top: capital city (over 1,000,000) · city (150,000–1,000,000) · large town (20,000–150,000) · small town (1,000–20,000) · village (up to 1,000) · hamlet (up to 20) · isolated dwelling (one family). Going up: bigger settlements and more services, but **fewer** settlements.
## Fieldwork (1.10)

**Fieldwork** = investigating a place first-hand: using maps, observation, photos and **field sketches** to collect, record and present data. Example: Seaford (East Sussex) – Seaford Head, Martello Tower, Seven Sisters chalk cliffs, **groynes** (human-made features to protect the beach) at Cuckmere Haven.
**Virtual fieldwork** (e.g. Google Street View of Keswick, Derwent Water) is safe, cheap and needs no travel, but you can't collect your own measurements and images may be out of date.

preguntas.enunciado: What is a vertical aerial photograph?
opciones: A photo taken from directly above
A photo taken from the side
A photo of a tall building
preguntas.explicacion: Usually from satellites or aeroplanes.

preguntas.enunciado: Most vertical aerial photographs today are taken from…
preguntas.explicacion: You can view them with Google Earth.

preguntas.enunciado: What is an urban area?
opciones: A built-up area such as a town or city
preguntas.explicacion: Most of the land is used for housing and industry.

preguntas.enunciado: What is a rural area?
preguntas.explicacion: Rural = countryside.

preguntas.enunciado: What is a model in geography?
opciones: A simplified version of a real-world pattern
A small plastic copy of a building
preguntas.explicacion: Models help make generalisations and predictions.

preguntas.enunciado: Why should geographers use models critically?
opciones: They have exceptions and can become out of date
They only work in the UK
preguntas.explicacion: Models have limitations.

preguntas.enunciado: What is a settlement?
preguntas.explicacion: Settlements vary in size from one house to huge cities.

preguntas.enunciado: Which is at the TOP of the UK settlement hierarchy?
preguntas.explicacion: Over 1,000,000 people.

preguntas.enunciado: A settlement has about 500 people, a church, a pub and a small primary school. What is it?
preguntas.explicacion: Village: up to 1,000 people.

preguntas.enunciado: What is the population of a hamlet in the UK model?
preguntas.explicacion: One family = isolated dwelling.

preguntas.enunciado: As you go UP the settlement hierarchy, the NUMBER of settlements…
preguntas.explicacion: There are many villages but few capital cities.

preguntas.enunciado: Willaston has about 2,500 people – more than a village but fewer than most small towns. What does this show about the model?
opciones: It is useful, but must be used with care
It is no help at all
preguntas.explicacion: Real places don't always fit models exactly.

preguntas.enunciado: What is a groyne?
opciones: A human-made feature to protect the beach
preguntas.explicacion: Groynes are at Seaford and Cuckmere Haven.

preguntas.enunciado: Which is an advantage of virtual fieldwork?
opciones: It is safe and you don't need to travel
You can measure the beach yourself
The images are always up to date
You can talk to local people
preguntas.explicacion: A disadvantage is that you can't collect your own data.

preguntas.enunciado: More than half of the world's population lives in urban areas.
preguntas.explicacion: In large towns and cities.

preguntas.enunciado: An isolated dwelling has a village hall and a shop.
preguntas.explicacion: Isolated dwellings (one family) have no services.

preguntas.enunciado: Put these in order from smallest to largest: city, hamlet, village, small town.
preguntas.explicacion: Check the pyramid.

preguntas.enunciado: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of virtual fieldwork.
preguntas.modelo: Advantage: it is safe, free and needs no travel. Disadvantage: you can't collect your own data and the images may be out of date.
preguntas.explicacion: Compare it with real fieldwork.
